caption:
Optical imagery cannot see through cloud. Radar can. That single fact decides which sensor is useful in West Africa's rainy season.

Optical sensors record reflected light — the same physics as a camera. Put a cloud deck between the sensor and the ground, and the pass returns nothing usable. Synthetic-aperture radar transmits its own microwave energy and measures what bounces back. Cloud is mostly transparent at that wavelength. The pass still returns ground truth.

This is not a resolution argument. A radar image is coarser than a clear-day optical shot. But a coarser image on the day you need it beats a sharp image you never get because the sky was overcast for six weeks straight — which is exactly the pattern during peak flood season.

Assessed: for any site where cloud cover is a recurring collection constraint, radar is the sensor that keeps the collection plan alive. Confirmed: optical still wins on interpretability when skies are clear. Unknown, for any given site: how many consecutive cloud-bound weeks it will see this year.

card.headline: Cloud stops light. Not radar.
card.sub: Optical imagery needs a clear sky. Synthetic-aperture radar reads its own return through cloud cover — coarser, but there when it matters.

rationale: Fills a clear EXPLAINER gap — cloud-penetration physics — without repeating cadence, false-positive, or backscatter angles already posted, and stays useful during the current rainy-season news cycle.
